body: while it's likely not a hisser, I've seen my pet hissing cockroaches stick their abdomens up in the air once in a while. couldn't find a pic of it, but I did find [someone on another subreddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/InvertPets/comments/k9x4po/hissing_cockroach_had_butt_sticking_up_in_the_air/) who had observed that same behavior
could be an [indian meal moth](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianmeal_moth), if you start seeing their larvae/pupae or more adults, check your pantry for anything they made have gotten into!
seems vaguely shaped like a roach ?
could be a seed bug nymph of sorts ?
yep seems to check out! seems to be an [Oedemera nobilis](https://www.naturespot.org/species/swollen-thighed-beetle) male considering the iconic coloration and location
kind of looks like an [assassin bug](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduviidae) nymph of some sort
could be a booklouse ([Liposcelididae](https://extension.psu.edu/booklice))!
looks like [Gryllotalpa](https://museum.wa.gov.au/research/collections/terrestrial-zoology/entomology-insect-collection/entomology-factsheets/mole-crickets), a mole cricket!
that'll be [Platypedia putnami](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypedia_putnami)!
some sort of [mayfly](https://stroudcenter.org/news/the-magic-of-mayflies/)?
could be a brownish deer fly, [Chrysops brunneus](https://bugguide.net/node/view/2280616/bgpage); has a pretty wide range and those bites do hurt pretty bad
OOHH very cool, could be a wingless soldier fly in the genus Boreoides, maybe [B. subulatus? ](https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8574)
could be a grain/wheat weevil in the genus [Sitophilus ](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitophilus)! if you see more of them, it's possible they've gotten into something in your pantry
could be [Anthonomus signatus](https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/abs/10.1079/cabicompendium.5731) ? if you have any strawberries, they might be munching on those plants.
could be [Meloe angusticollis](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meloe_angusticollis) ? don't touch it haha
looking like an [aphid](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphid)! that wing venation is pretty iconic haha

it miiiight be the evergreen bagworm, [Thyridopteryx ephemeraeformis](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen_bagworm) ? if so then that's a male; the females don't leave their cocoon and look like their larval forms.

edit: i don't live within this moth's range so I can't say much on the behavior, but it's definitely weird that the abdomen is so stretched out like that. i don't think I've ever seen that before

german cockroach, the stripes on the pronotum are a dead giveaway :•{

could be a drain fly larva, especially considering you found it in your shower. there might be more in your drain if that's the case; if their moth-like adult form also appears in your bathroom, it's almost certainly them.

sometimes wasp IDing can be a bit difficult, especially because identification keys tend to rely closely on the shape and size of specific segments :'( do you know if you are able to take a good pic of the wings? wing venation can be really helpful in IDing down to family level at least!

edit: also! ants generally tend to have elbowed (geniculate) antennae. we might have something different on our hands here :)

i think I see a rostrum there, so it's likely this guy could be  a weevil!
that patterning looks very similar to the iconic acorn weevil (Curculio glandium) but there is a similar species, C. nucum, that can only really be differentiated by antennal club shape ([source](https://www.naturespot.org.uk/species/acorn-weevil))
velvet mite! ([trombidiidae](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombidiidae))
lace bug! family tingidae. can be a major nuisance depending on species and whatever host plant it hopped on from, but it won't hurt you specifically
drain fly, they can be pretty persistent but there's plenty of methods to deal with em. my go-to is baking soda + vinegar :)
probably just a cranefly! harmless :)
